read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 1d2470eb356b, store_version 3d8c4ef86c01 (its index.json), for "Strong's Hebrew concordance with explicit source form lists via Hebrew Wikisource" (M14): 148,343 routes (axis: routes), 17,003 letters keys (axis: keys), of which 107,637 routes hold no mark. The definition field of the same row is read only to understand a route, never classified: it equals the route text on 3 routes, and every route text stands inside its definition; the store's cut flag stands on 513 routes. In this ledger "the source" and "the edition" mean the Hebrew Wikisource edition of Strong's that the store holds (the dictionary store's records/M14.jsonl, 5,806 records, one per Strong's entry), and "the print" means the book whose scan that edition's own index page names as the photograph of the dictionary: <tabernacle>/corpus-lane-builds/moses-works-own-stamp-v1/strand-1-the-old-books/fetch/M14-strongs-concise-dictionary-scan-named-by-wikisource.pdf, read by its text layer, which is OCR. The source's own key to its signs is the print's front matter, found by that index page and on file in <tabernacle>/corpus-lane-builds/moses-works-own-stamp-v1/strand-1-the-old-books/fetch/M14-strongs-scan-first12pages.txt: PLAN OF THE BOOK, item 6 at line 59 (after the punctuation-mark :-- come the renderings of the Authorized Version, conveniently condensed), with items 4 and 5 before it; HEBREW ARTICULATION from line 82 (Aleph the apostrophe at line 104, Ayin a reversed apostrophe); ABBREVIATIONS EMPLOYED at line 165; SIGNS EMPLOYED from line 284 (the plus sign, the multiplication sign, the parenthesis, the bracket and italics). Of the 119 shapes, 76 name the print in their meaning, and those are written from it; 14 begin "unverified:", each for its reason: open_paren.never_closed, close_paren.never_opened: the print's key speaks of a bracket's use, not of a bracket with no partner; open_paren.holds_verse_citation, close_paren.holds_verse_citation: the print has such citations, and its key does not speak of them; open_paren.holds_note, close_paren.holds_note: the print has these notes in square brackets, its bracket line speaks of an additional word, and its line on italics may be their key; the scan's images could not be read here, and the text layer and the edition show no italics; comma.in_unbalanced_text: the print's key does not speak of a text whose brackets do not balance; period.in_run_of_dots, period.paren_in_run_of_dots: the print has the dots and says no word of them; ampersand.stands_before_a_word: the print has no such sign at these texts, so nothing on file says what the edition's sign is for; hyphen.in_unbalanced_text: the print's key speaks of a syllable, not of a hyphen in a compound or of a text whose brackets do not balance; hyphen.joins_compound, hyphen.paren_joins_compound: the print's key does not speak of a hyphen in a compound; hyphen.paren_stands_alone_before_closer: the print's key does not speak of a hyphen with no letter of its own; and 29 do neither, because they say what a mark does in the text and claim no sign of the key: the 13 Hebrew marks, and comma.paren_in_note_or_sentence, semicolon.opens_text, semicolon.before_second_sense_in_sentence, semicolon.before_second_sense_after_pointer, semicolon.between_spellings, semicolon.before_label_that_stands_alone, semicolon.paren_in_note_or_sentence, period.in_unbalanced_text, period.before_note_after_rendering, period.paren_ends_note, period.paren_after_book_abbreviation, period.paren_ends_sentence_in_note, colon.in_verse_citation, question_mark.ends_question_word, apostrophe.marks_possessive, quote.around_cited_words. The print differs from the edition, by its text layer (edition / print): --Aharhel, / Aharhel. · (make) crooked. / (make) crooked, · with(-in.) / with (-in). · d-fierce / fierce. · -swiftly.e / swiftly. · member.ql / member. · -Jeuz.(gl / Jeuz. · & presume / presume · lay & to (take a) pledge / lay to (take a) pledge · landmark. place / landmark, place · thing. word / thing, word · Ludim. Lydians / Ludim, Lydians · (give to, leave for) inherit(-ance, -or) + magistrate / (give to, leave for) inherit (-ance, -or), + magistrate; the semicolon of the dividing shape is a comma in the print at 7 of its 11 texts. The print's square bracket: its text layer holds 755 square-bracket groups of 40 characters or fewer, and the edition's characters hold none, so named_cases.brackets is absent as to the edition's characters only: the edition writes that sign as a doubled round bracket (the print has the square bracket at 73 of the 76 texts with one) or as one round bracket (at least 156 distinct contents), so the round-bracket shapes under named_cases.parentheses hold the print's two signs merged: of 38,613 aligned occurrences of the seven shapes whose meanings give the figure, 2,879 have the square bracket at the place, a floor, because a misread sign counts as neither. That the words after the sentence are the King James list rests on the print's plan and on the sister copy of the same work, openscriptures_strongs, whose file names its usage field (figures in the relay). The route text names neither the part of the entry it came from nor the entry's number; the lane read both from the record by audit (builder/source-audit.mjs), which is evidence about the source and no part of any test. Of the routes 145,847 stand after the point where the list opens, 2,229 before it, 123 across it and 37 in a definition with no such point (axis: routes; the relay states the steps).

definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file, and the first whose test holds names the occurrence. This holds for every test of this file, whether or not the test names first_match, so every test speaks only of the occurrences that no shape above it, for the same mark, has taken, and a short test relies on that. Not caught above means exactly that. A mark that no test takes would make the template throw; no route here does.
definitions.terms: A character is one Unicode code point of the text; no route holds a character above U+FFFF, so every character is also one JavaScript string unit, and a length is a count of either. A letter is any character of Unicode general category L, of any script. A digit is any character of category N. Whitespace is any character the JavaScript class \s matches. A Hebrew letter is a character from U+05D0 to U+05EA. Trimmed means with whitespace removed at both ends. The text is the route text as served, untrimmed. Begins with compares characters from the start and needs no word end after them; ends with likewise from the end. Contains means a run of characters anywhere, with no word end. Equals compares two whole strings, character for character. Every comparison and every list minds case; no test asks for an uppercase or a lowercase letter as a class, and a test that names one letter names its case. Directly before and directly after mean the one character next to the mark, with nothing between; at the start or the end of the text there is no such character, so a test that asks for one fails. Top level means the template's c.container is top; inside round brackets means the template's c.container is paren. Every string of a list is written in definitions in full; the JSON quotes are not part of it, and every character inside them belongs to the string, a stop or a space at its end too.
definitions.unbalanced: The ask's helper, rule 3, copied byte for byte into the classifier as the function unbalanced(text). Read the text from left to right with a stack: push each of the opening brackets ( [ < { ; at each of the closing brackets ) ] > } , if the top of the stack is its partner pop it, and otherwise the answer is true at once; at the end the answer is true if the stack is not empty, and false if it is. Only round brackets occur in these routes.
definitions.pair_words: An opening or closing round bracket and its partner are a pair, by the template's own matching. What the pair holds is the template's c.group: the text between the two, untrimmed, the same for the opener and for the closer. before_pair is the text before the opener of the pair; after_pair is the text after the closer of the pair. For an opener, after_pair is c.after without its first (c.group's length plus one) string units; for a closer, before_pair is c.before without its last (c.group's length plus one) string units.
definitions.sentence_text: A text is a sentence_text when it contains a semicolon and does not equal one of two_renderings_texts. Such a text was read route by route against the record: it comes from the source's sentence about the word, joins that sentence to a King James word, or holds a note after the list.
definitions.whole_bracket_text: Holds for a string G when the text, trimmed, equals an opening round bracket, then G, then a closing round bracket; or equals the capital letter X, one space character, an opening round bracket, G and a closing round bracket.
definitions.one_inner_bracket: Holds for a string G when G begins with an opening round bracket, ends with a closing round bracket, and that closing bracket is the partner of that opening bracket: walking through G and counting each opening round bracket up and each closing one down, the count first comes back to zero at the last character of G.
definitions.pair_kind: One step list for an opener and for its closer. G is what the pair holds; the first step that holds gives the kind. (1) The template's c.depth is above 0: the kind is inner_end if G, with the whitespace at its start removed, begins with a hyphen; otherwise inner_start if G, with the whitespace at its end removed, ends with a hyphen; otherwise inner_words. c.depth counts only pairs that close: an opener that never closes is not counted, so a pair after such an opener stands at c.depth 0 and goes on to step 2, even where the eye reads it as inside that opener. This is what the test means. Steps 2 onward are for a pair at c.depth 0. (2) citation: G contains a digit directly followed by a colon directly followed by a digit. (3) note: G begins with one of note_openers. (4) label: G equals one of bracket_labels. (5) sentence: the text is a sentence_text. (6) sign: G, trimmed, equals one of bracket_signs. (7) whole: whole_bracket_text holds for G. (8) doubled: one_inner_bracket holds for G. (9) choices: G contains a comma, at any depth inside G. (10) word_end: G, with the whitespace at its start removed, begins with a hyphen. (11) word_start: G, with the whitespace at its end removed, ends with a hyphen. (12) against: the last character of before_pair is a letter, or the first character of after_pair is a letter. (13) words_first: before_pair, trimmed, is empty, or equals the capital letter X, or equals the plus sign, or equals one hyphen. (14) words_last: after_pair, trimmed, is empty. (15) words_between: any other pair.
definitions.holder: For a comma inside round brackets: the three tests that name holder say so. Walk back from the comma through the text before it, counting each closing round bracket up and each opening one down; the first opening round bracket met at count zero holds the comma, and before_holder is the text before it (empty if none is met). Walk forward from the comma through the text after it, counting each opening round bracket up and each closing one down; the first closing round bracket met at count zero is its partner, and after_holder is the text after it (empty if none is met).
definitions.clause_before: The text between the last semicolon before the mark, wherever that semicolon stands, inside round brackets or not, and the mark, trimmed; if there is no semicolon before the mark, the text from the start of the text to the mark, trimmed.
definitions.in_ie: A full stop is in_ie when the text before it ends with the three characters i, full stop, e (the second stop of i.e.), or when the text before it ends with the letter i and the text after it begins with the two characters e, full stop (the first stop of i.e.).
definitions.word_before_stop: The longest run of letters that ends directly before the full stop; empty if the character directly before the stop is not a letter.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The key is a word form (the source lists the forms of each entry with their verses) and the routes of a key are the renderings of each entry that holds the form, so one key can hold the list of one entry or of several. The record gives every entry a heading with its Strong's number, which the store dropped, and two entries under one letters key stand there as separate texts with nothing to tell them apart (example key אדר: its entries in the record are H142 and H145, and its 4 route texts come from those two). keys_with_more_than_one_route_text counts renderings, senses and homonyms together. By the audit, of the 14,353 such keys (axis: keys; 17,003 letters keys in all) 11,798 take every text from one definition and 2,555 from two or more.

branches.question: The print ends its sentence about a word with the sign :-- and then gives the King James renderings. In some texts of the Wikisource edition a semicolon stands before the dash there, so sentence and rendering share one text. Two of those are asked here, where each part stands alone, like: or (abstractly) capture; also a fastness; --castle. Should they be separate readings? Every other such text stays one reading under either answer: what stands before the sign holds a pointer, an origin label, a spelling, a restatement after i.e., a name's description or a remark, or leans on earlier routes, or a note follows (excrement; -dung. Also chariy). So do meanings inside one round bracket.

options.means: The page prints or (abstractly) capture, also a fastness and --castle as three readings, and continually (i.e. to the most distant point of view) and --alway(-s) as two. The semicolon at a cut is left out, as a comma is, and the dash stays on the word.
The page prints each text as one reading, as the source writes it: or (abstractly) capture; also a fastness; --castle.

branches.question: In three texts of the Wikisource edition a full stop stands between the last two King James words, where the print has a comma, like: thing. word. Should the full stop divide them into two readings?

options.means: The full stop cuts: the page prints thing and word as two readings, and the stop at the cut is left out, as a comma is.
The full stop does not cut: the page prints thing. word as one reading, as written.

branches.question: In some texts of the Wikisource edition a semicolon stands between two King James words, like: chap(-man); divers. The ledger lists these whole texts by hand, because no test can find them, so they wait for you. Should the two words be separate readings? Today the page cuts at that semicolon and prints chap(-man) and divers as two pills. From the day this is wired it prints what you answer, and one reading until you answer.

options.means: The semicolon cuts: the page prints chap(-man) and divers as two readings, and the semicolon at the cut is left out, as a comma is.
The semicolon does not cut: the page prints chap(-man); divers as one reading, as the source writes it.

not_done_here: This ledger leaves to the route store the cutting of the source's list at its commas outside brackets, which gave each rendering its own route except in the 0 definitions whose first route stands after a verse colon and whose list before it is in no route (0 keys, 0 routes, in lost-lists-v1.tsv, a question for the store), so a bracket or a word end that the cut left alone, whose rendering stands in another route of the same definition, next to it at all but 13 of 186 routes (axis: routes), and a text whose round brackets do not balance (187 routes: 88 real lists, 0 note, 99 with no comma) stay as the store gives them; it holds whole a note after a rendering, and a pointer or a restatement before one, which wait for the note piece of version 1.2 of the ask; it gives no shape to the capital X, the print's multiplication sign, because a letter is no mark under the ask (11,874 routes hold it standing alone), nor to a comma the edition has lost where no mark stands to cut (a floor of 9 texts, 80 routes); and a pointer at the end of a text stays in the last piece, though no route that divides at rest here ends in one (0 by count).
